dailyBrief.text: Good morning, Smileys — and an extra hour of morning, since the clocks fell back overnight. It's a cloudy, mild Sunday in Solon, high near 68°, and the overnight sports split the house: the Cavs rolled 136–111 in Milwaukee behind Mobley and Allen, while Ohio State fell 30–18 at USC with freshman Luke Fahey starting for the injured Julian Sayin. Overseas, Iran claimed tankers hit mines in the Strait of Hormuz — a story Washington calls false and Iran's own Guards deny — with oil holding near $117. Today is stacked: the Browns play at Pittsburgh at 1 PM for first place in the AFC North, and it is the final day of early voting, 1 to 5 PM at the Cuyahoga County Board of Elections, before Tuesday's midterms. And the biggest story of all is still your own — after last night's trip to the hospital, everyone here is thinking of Kelly and the baby.

weekBrief.text: The week ahead in Solon starts mild and turns wet: cloudy and about 63° Monday, the warmest day of the week Tuesday at about 73° for Election Day, then showers build Wednesday, rain is likely Thursday, and a sharp cooldown drops Friday into the low 50s. Election week frames everything — early voting ends today at 5 PM, polls are open Tuesday 6:30 AM to 7:30 PM (66 Cuyahoga precincts have moved, so check yours), and the governor's and Senate races top a long ballot. In sports, the Browns play at Pittsburgh today for first place, the Cavs — fresh off a 136–111 rout in Milwaukee — host Oklahoma City Monday night, and Ohio State looks to regroup after Saturday's loss at USC. The standout deal remains Giant Eagle's BOGO-free sirloin tip roasts through Wednesday — and at home, with Kelly's labor starting last night, this is the week the Smiley family very likely grows by one.

items.title: Cavs vs Oklahoma City Thunder
Iran says the Strait of Hormuz could reopen in two days if the U.S. meets its terms
items.summary:
Iran's foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, said Sunday that talks with Qatari mediators have produced a proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within two days if the United States carries out Tehran's conditions. That is a shorter timeline than the five days floated earlier, and Araghchi presented it as a route back to direct negotiations with Washington.

The conditions are extensive. Tehran wants sanctions imposed after the collapse of the Islamabad agreement in July lifted, a smaller American military presence in the region, the oil waivers granted in June restored, and frozen Iranian funds released, including money held in Qatar. Iran also wants agreement on a shipping route through the strait discussed with Oman, and an end to the fighting on other fronts, especially Israeli attacks in Lebanon. A senior security official, Mohsen Rezaei, said there would be no talks and no reopening unless Iran's conditions are met.

Hormuz is the world's most important oil chokepoint, so even a conditional offer moves markets and shipping decisions. The proposal is the clearest timeline Iran has offered, but it depends on demands Washington has not accepted, and it arrived alongside a letter from Vice President JD Vance that Tehran described as a positive shift in tone. No direct meeting with American officials is currently planned.

Watch for Iran's formal answer to the mediators, a third day of talks in Doha, and any American decision on renewed strikes after Tuesday's midterms.

items.title: Iran's supreme leader orders a maximum response, with no geographic limits, to any new U.S. attack
items.summary:
Iran's supreme leader, Mojtaba Khamenei, met his three senior military commanders and ordered an immediate and effective response, without geographic limits, to any renewed American or Israeli attack. Axios reported it was the first publicly disclosed meeting between Khamenei and all three commanders since the war began, and he said Iran, not its enemies, would decide when hostilities end.

At the table were Armed Forces Chief of Staff Ali Abdollahi, Army Commander Amir Hatami and Revolutionary Guards Commander Ahmad Vahidi. They briefed him on readiness along the Persian Gulf coast, in the Strait of Hormuz and the Gulf of Oman, and on other borders, and reported that weapons and ammunition production has grown. Khamenei directed them to update Iran's target list to include American and Israeli assets of every kind.

The order landed while diplomacy was still running. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is pressing President Trump to resume strikes right after Tuesday's midterms, according to Axios, while Trump has said he wants more time for negotiations. That puts a standing threat of wider retaliation next to a live negotiating track.

Watch the first American signals after the election, and whether the Qatari channel produces a step that lowers the chance of another round.

items.title: Russian strikes cut power to hundreds of thousands in Ukraine as both sides hit energy targets
items.summary:
Russia attacked power infrastructure in four Ukrainian regions overnight, leaving hundreds of thousands of households without electricity on Sunday, President Volodymyr Zelensky said. Ukraine's air force said it shot down 371 of 433 long-range drones launched since Saturday evening, and Kyiv went through repeated drone alerts after midnight.

Ukraine struck back at scale. Russia said it intercepted 235 Ukrainian drones overnight, and the governor of the Nizhny Novgorod region acknowledged significant damage to an industrial facility he did not name. The region hosts a major refinery at Kstovo, where a fire was reported. Zelensky also said Ukrainian forces hit the Kamensky plant in the Rostov region, which he said produces Russian missiles.

Both sides are now treating energy as a central front heading into winter. Russia is trying to deepen Ukraine's power shortage, while Ukraine is trying to make the war felt in Russian fuel supplies. Russia's deputy prime minister for energy conceded that the refinery strikes are adding to imbalances in fuel markets.

Watch whether emergency outages in Ukraine turn into longer rolling blackouts this week, and whether fuel shortages spread in Russia.

items.title: A rare ceasefire in Kherson expires Sunday evening, and civilians brace for fighting to return
items.summary:
A localized ceasefire in Ukraine's Kherson region, described as the most significant truce since Russia's full-scale invasion began four and a half years ago, was set to end Sunday evening. The pause began early Tuesday and allowed a rare joint evacuation operation around the town of Oleshky.

Oleshky sits on the Russian-occupied left bank of the Dnipro River, and about 2,000 civilians, including roughly 50 children, were there when the truce took hold. Evacuees could choose Ukrainian- or Russian-controlled territory, or stay with fresh food and medical supplies. The evacuation finished Saturday. The White House says First Lady Melania Trump helped broker the pause.

The relief was local and temporary. Local officials warn Russian forces used the quiet to bring in more weapons and personnel, and fighting continued elsewhere in Ukraine during the truce, including a drone strike on a vocational school in Vinnytsia that killed two people.

Watch for any last-minute extension. As of Sunday, neither Moscow nor Kyiv had announced one.

items.title: Serbia votes again at 53 polling stations after a student-backed list's shock election win
items.summary:
Serbia held repeat voting on Sunday at 53 polling stations in 24 towns, covering about 24,400 eligible voters, after problems in last weekend's early parliamentary elections. Fresh voting was ordered where results could not be determined or where voting had been cancelled.

Preliminary results from most stations put the student-backed coalition ahead with about 52.7 percent, against about 39.2 percent for the list led by President Aleksandar Vucic's Serbian Progressive Party. A total of 18 lists contested 250 seats in the National Assembly, with about 6.45 million voters registered.

A student victory would end roughly 14 years of dominance by Vucic's party after years of anti-government protests. Vucic dissolved parliament in September, called the election, and then resigned as president, leaving the speaker as acting president and a presidential election due by the end of December.

Watch for certified final results after the repeat voting, and then how quickly a new government can be formed.

items.title: More than 300,000 people flee fighting in western Yemen, the U.N. says
items.summary:
More than 300,000 people have fled their homes in western Yemen as fighting intensifies between Houthi forces and Saudi-backed government troops, the International Organization for Migration said Sunday. Almost all of that displacement has happened in the past two months.

The agency said displaced families urgently need shelter, food, clean water and health care, and that it needs about $45 million over the next six months to keep emergency help going. Thousands of Yemenis had already fled across the sea to Djibouti in September as the fighting spread.

The surge adds another major humanitarian crisis in the same region as the Iran war and the disruption in the Strait of Hormuz. It strains aid budgets that are already stretched, and fighting in western Yemen also affects security around the Red Sea shipping routes.

Watch for the funding response, and whether fighting around the western coast pushes more people toward the ports and border crossings.

items.title: Trump heads to Iowa and Kansas for final rallies two days before the midterms
items.summary:
President Trump returned to the campaign trail on Sunday with rallies in Dubuque, Iowa, and Salina, Kansas, two Republican-leaning Farm Belt states where his party is fighting to hold Senate seats. The stops came two days before midterms that will decide control of Congress.

Trump won Iowa by double digits in 2024, but polls now show Democrats tied or leading in several Iowa races, and his approval among rural Americans fell to a new low of 45 percent in October in Reuters/Ipsos polling. Kansas, which last elected a Democratic senator in 1932, also has a closer-than-expected Senate race. All 435 House seats and 35 Senate seats are on the ballot.

Republicans hold a 53-47 Senate majority and a narrow House edge. Losing either chamber would let Democrats block Trump's agenda for his final two years and open investigations. Early voting has already passed 52 million ballots, a midterm record.

Watch Tuesday's turnout in the Farm Belt races, and Trump's planned remarks in Washington on Monday.

items.title: The White House is mapping how to govern without Congress if Democrats win
items.summary:
Trump's White House has spent months preparing for a possible Democratic takeover of Congress, building plans to advance major parts of his agenda through executive power while bracing for investigations, Reuters reported Sunday, citing a White House official and two people familiar with the work.

Since April, senior aides including Stephen Miller and budget director Russell Vought, along with the White House counsel's office, have catalogued actions that need no vote in Congress. The list includes possible new tariffs on critical minerals and wind turbines, tighter visa rules for international students and temporary workers, and steps on housing and construction costs. Vought is also reviewing how already-appropriated money and grant rules could give political appointees more control over spending.

Democrats need a net gain of four seats to flip either chamber. Polls favor them for the House, while the Senate is too close to call. Even a Democratic Congress could not easily stop executive action on trade, foreign policy and the federal workforce, though it could block nominees, refuse legislation and investigate, and White House lawyers are already preparing appointees for subpoenas.

Watch for the first executive actions after Tuesday if Democrats win a chamber, and the court fights that would follow.

items.title: A judge throws out Trump's $10 billion lawsuit against The Wall Street Journal, for good
items.summary:
A federal judge in Miami has dismissed President Trump's $10 billion lawsuit against The Wall Street Journal and Rupert Murdoch, and dismissed it with prejudice, meaning it cannot be refiled. Judge Darrin Gayles said the president was grasping at straws and had tried to manufacture flaws in the Journal's reporting.

The case grew out of a 2025 Journal story about a sexually suggestive letter bearing Trump's name in a 2003 album compiled for Jeffrey Epstein's 50th birthday. Trump denied writing it and sued days later. To win, he had to show the paper acted with actual malice, meaning it knew the story was false or acted with reckless disregard for the truth. Gayles ruled the amended complaint fell short and noted the Journal's story itself reported Trump's denial.

This was the second dismissal in the case. The first came in April, and Trump was allowed to refile in May, but the new version failed for the same reason. An appeal remains possible, but the district-court case is over.

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Watch whether Trump appeals during midterm week.

items.title: Early voting passes 51 million as ballot fights heat up in Alaska and California
items.summary:
More than 51 million Americans had cast ballots by Saturday, a midterm early-voting record, as the campaign entered its final weekend with legal fights running alongside the rallies. The total is up from about 46 million in all of 2022, and later counts put it above 52 million.

In Alaska, federal prosecutors are investigating whether aides to Democratic Senate challenger Mary Peltola helped recruit a retired teacher with a name similar to Republican Senator Dan Sullivan to run as a spoiler. Peltola's campaign and the other candidate deny any coordination. In California, a federal appeals court ruled that the Justice Department had not justified setting aside mail ballots from more than 20,000 voters, and a department official said the Supreme Court is probably next.

Alaska is central to Democrats' hopes of taking the Senate, and the California fight tests how far the federal government can go in challenging state ballot rules in the final days before an election. The administration has sued roughly 30 states and Washington, D.C., for unredacted voter rolls.

Watch for a Supreme Court filing on California before Tuesday, and the final early-vote totals.

items.title: A Democrat who lost Michigan's Senate primary endorses the Republican nominee
items.summary:
Representative Haley Stevens, who narrowly lost Michigan's Democratic Senate primary to Abdul El-Sayed, endorsed his Republican opponent, former Representative Mike Rogers, on Sunday, two days before Election Day. She appeared with Rogers at a prominent Detroit church and said she does not belong in El-Sayed's campaign.

Stevens had been expected at a unity event with El-Sayed, but that plan collapsed after she demanded he condemn an outside group's ad and criticized his campaign. She called herself a very proud Democrat while breaking with her party's nominee. Trump welcomed the endorsement, while Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer called it a betrayal, Michigan's Democratic chair said Stevens is no longer a party member, and her longtime chief of staff said he and other staff had resigned.

Michigan's open Senate seat is one of the most closely watched races in the country, and no Republican has won it since 1994. Polling averages had El-Sayed ahead by roughly four points before the endorsement, in a chamber Republicans currently lead 53-47.

Watch whether the endorsement moves late undecided voters, and how Michigan votes on Tuesday.

items.title: Trump says he will become 'Mr. Veto' if Democrats win Congress
items.summary:
President Trump said he would become 'Mr. Veto' if Democrats take control of Congress on Tuesday, vowing to block their bills until they come to make deals. He made the remark on a New York Post podcast, in a clip aired Sunday ahead of the full episode on Monday.

Trump said Democrats would send bills up, he would veto them, and after a month or two they would come over to negotiate. He has vetoed only two bills in his second term, compared with ten in his first. Overriding a veto takes two-thirds of both chambers, a bar neither party is close to reaching.

The comment is a rare public acknowledgment that Republicans could lose. Forecasters favor Democrats to win back the House, while the Senate is rated a toss-up, with competitive Republican-held races in states including Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Ohio and Texas.

Watch the full podcast episode on Monday, and whether Trump's final-day message stays on vetoes and dealmaking or shifts back to turnout.

items.title: OpenAI wants to call data centers 'AI compute campuses' in a post-midterm push
items.summary:
OpenAI is preparing a policy and public-relations push to start right after Tuesday's midterms, Axios reported, including a proposal to call its big facilities AI compute campuses instead of data centers. The company's global affairs chief, Chris Lehane, said the midterms will be a preview of 2028, when he expects artificial intelligence to be the central issue.

The plans, assembled since August, include mandatory safeguards for the most powerful systems that Lehane calls speed limits, help for workers and small businesses, and community agreements that give local residents a say in how projects are built. The push would begin in the lame-duck session of Congress that opens November 9. It follows a campaign season in which about $173 million in general-election ads mentioned data centers, almost all of them negative.

Data centers have become a local political fight in much of the country, including in Ohio, where a large OpenAI project is planned. Language alone will not settle fights over power, water and land, but OpenAI is trying to keep gigawatt-scale building politically possible ahead of a likely Democratic House.

Watch for the first concrete proposals after November 9, and whether other companies adopt the new name.

items.title: OpenAI cuts its fundraising target to $20 billion as big investors cool on AI
items.summary:
OpenAI has cut the funding round it is trying to close from about $30 billion to $20 billion, and lowered its target valuation from $1.4 trillion to $1.25 trillion, according to Financial Times reporting summarized Sunday. Some large investors trimmed or shrank their commitments ahead of Friday's deadline, and the first close is now expected to come in below the reduced target.

Investors from the United Arab Emirates, including the state-backed fund MGX, are expected to provide the largest share, alongside firms such as Coatue, Founders Fund, Sequoia and Andreessen Horowitz. Earlier reporting put the amount secured at roughly $11 billion as of last week. OpenAI did not comment in the reports.

The cut landed in the middle of an AI selloff, with the Nasdaq 100 down 3.46 percent on Friday. OpenAI is also racing its rival Anthropic, which is heading toward a market debut, for the same pool of investor money while its spending commitments for computing keep growing.

Watch the final close figure. Investors will read it as a verdict on how much of the AI buildout they are still willing to fund.

items.title: Anthropic's IPO filing shows $16.3 billion in half-year revenue and a huge paper loss
items.summary:
Anthropic's public filing for its stock-market debut shows revenue of $16.3 billion in the first half of 2026, up sharply from a year earlier, with its second quarter alone beating all of its 2025 revenue. The filing, submitted October 26, sets up what could be one of the largest initial public offerings ever, with trading expected the week of November 16 under the ticker ANT.

The headline net loss of about $80.7 billion is mostly a non-cash charge of roughly $72 billion tied to the value of convertible notes. Underneath that, the operating loss for the half year was far smaller, and one quarter showed an operating profit. The filing also lays out about $518 billion in planned computing spending over the next decade and large contracts with Google, Amazon, Microsoft, Broadcom and others. The company runs on cloud services rather than its own data centers.

For investors, the filing is the first detailed look at the economics of a leading AI lab: very fast growth, enormous future computing bills, and a share structure that leaves the seven cofounders with just over half the voting power.

Watch for the price range, which has not yet been disclosed, when marketing begins the week of November 9.

items.title: Tech stocks lose more than $1 trillion as AI spending worries hit earnings week
items.summary:
Friday's selloff erased more than $1 trillion from technology valuations. The S&P 500 fell 1.82 percent to 7,580.07, the Dow fell 1.09 percent, and the Nasdaq 100 fell 3.46 percent, in the steepest broad decline since June.

Alphabet and Amazon led the drop. Alphabet's advertising revenue came in below estimates and its net income fell, while Amazon reported negative free cash flow alongside very large capital spending in the quarter. Chip makers Nvidia and AMD also fell. Energy was an offset, with Exxon and Chevron beating expectations.

The pattern is a change in what investors are rewarding. For two years, bigger AI spending plans were treated as good news. Now spending without a clear return is being penalized, which is the same pressure behind OpenAI's smaller funding round and the questions facing Anthropic's debut.

Watch Apple and Palantir earnings after Monday's close, the jobs report on Friday, and Nvidia's results later in November.

items.title: Samsung posts the first 100-trillion-won profit quarter ever, driven almost entirely by AI memory
items.summary:
Samsung reported third-quarter operating profit of 107.4 trillion won, the first time any technology company has passed 100 trillion won in a single quarter, and its fourth straight record quarter. Revenue was 195.3 trillion won, more than double a year earlier.

Almost all of it came from chips. The semiconductor division earned 106.5 trillion won of the total, memory revenue rose sharply, and sales of its newest high-bandwidth memory more than tripled from the previous quarter. Ordinary phone and television businesses lost money in the quarter, squeezed in part by the same expensive memory. Samsung said its 2027 supply of high-bandwidth memory is already sold out.

The result shows where the bottleneck in the AI buildout really sits. Memory has become the commodity everyone needs, which gives Samsung pricing power and raises costs for every company building or buying AI systems.

Watch Samsung's January board meeting on shareholder returns, and any sign that memory prices ease in 2027 contracts.

items.title: Big AI firms agree on one shared way for websites to opt out of AI training
items.summary:
OpenAI, Google, Microsoft and Anthropic have agreed to honor a single signal that lets a website say whether its pages may be used to train AI systems. Instead of blocking each company's crawler separately, a site can add one entry to its robots.txt file covering AI training.

The proposal was submitted to an internet standards group by an Anthropic engineer, and it is still a draft, not a finished standard. The companies are adopting it on different schedules: Anthropic says it supports it now, Microsoft from February 2027, Google in early 2027, and OpenAI in the coming months. It covers future training only, and does not block crawling for search.

Publishers have spent years fighting scraping company by company, including in court. One shared signal lowers that friction, but the staggered timelines, and the fact that Meta has not committed to it, mean the fight is not over.

Watch whether the draft becomes a formal standard, and how it interacts with the crawler-specific blocks sites already use.

items.title: Trump's noncitizen voter lists could be used to challenge close midterm results
items.summary:
As voters head to the polls Tuesday, lists of possible noncitizen voters assembled by the Trump administration could be used to contest close results. The Justice Department has acknowledged sending letters to several states, and in California it demanded that ballots from about 20,000 voters not be counted without verification.

Federal courts have pushed back. A judge rejected the department's bid on October 28, saying it would wreak havoc, and an appeals court upheld that ruling on October 30, citing the risk of disenfranchising eligible voters, since many people on the lists are citizens. The department has obtained at least partial voter-roll data from at least 47 states and is suing states that have not handed over unredacted rolls.

Reuters found only 129 federal charges for illegal voting by noncitizens since 1996, many involving confusion or administrative errors. That gap between the scale of the lists and the record of actual cases is at the center of the legal argument.

Watch for a Supreme Court filing before Tuesday, and for certification challenges in any race decided by a small margin.

items.title: A debut winner and a repeat champion take the New York City Marathon as 60,000 run
items.summary:
Sweden's Andreas Almgren won the men's New York City Marathon on Sunday in 2 hours, 6 minutes and 1 second, in the first marathon of his career. Kenya's Sheila Chepkirui won the women's race in 2:24:36, her second New York title after 2024.

Almgren pulled away in the final mile and finished 13 seconds ahead of Italy's Yemaneberhan Crippa, in the third-fastest time in the race's five-borough history. American Jessica McClain finished second in the women's race, passing two-time champion Hellen Obiri in the final strides, the first American woman on the podium since 2018. Marcel Hug won his eighth wheelchair title.

About 60,000 people started the race, nearly half of them women, from more than 140 countries, in a record field for the 50th running of the five-borough course. The course itself changed slightly in the Bronx for the first time in 15 years.

The marathon closes the fall major season, with Valencia on December 6 the next big international race.

items.title: Clocks fell back today as daylight saving time ended, and Congress is still debating the switch
items.summary:
Daylight saving time ended at 2 a.m. on Sunday, when clocks went back to 1 a.m. and most Americans gained an hour of sleep. Standard time now runs until March 14, 2027, with lighter mornings and darker evenings.

The current dates, from the second Sunday in March to the first Sunday in November, date to a 2005 law that took effect in 2007. Hawaii and most of Arizona do not observe the change, along with U.S. territories. The switch this year came the morning after Halloween.

Congress is still arguing about ending it. The House passed a bill in July, by 308 to 117, to make daylight saving time permanent, and President Trump has pressed the Senate to act. Senators from northern states have raised concerns about dark winter mornings for commutes and school, and the Senate has not voted.

Watch for any Senate action before the end of the year. Without it, the next change is March 14, 2027.

items.title: A warm start to November gives way to severe storms, flash flooding and Rockies snow
items.summary:
Unseasonable warmth is surging across the central and eastern United States to start November, with temperatures 10 to 20 degrees above average from Texas to Minnesota on Monday and 80s in Texas and Louisiana. By Tuesday the warmth reaches the Ohio Valley, the Great Lakes and the Northeast, ahead of a cold front.

That front brings the week's weather risks. About 48 million people in at least 17 states face a risk of excessive rainfall and flash flooding on Monday into early Tuesday, with the highest chances on Florida's Atlantic coast. More than 21 million people face a risk of severe storms on Monday, mainly damaging winds and large hail, with a few tornadoes possible.

In the West, snow is aimed at high elevations in Montana, Wyoming, Utah and Colorado. A winter storm warning covers southwest Colorado until noon Monday, with 12 to 18 inches expected above 10,000 feet and gusts to 45 miles per hour.

Forecasters expect Election Day itself to be mostly manageable, with light rain in New England and showers in Florida the main issues for voters on Tuesday.

items.title: Exxon and Chevron post surging profits as the Iran war lifts oil earnings again
items.summary:
America's two biggest oil companies reported sharply higher third-quarter profits, helped by the Iran war's effect on oil and refining markets. Exxon reported about $15.4 billion in profit, roughly double a year earlier, and Chevron reported about $9.9 billion, up from about $3.5 billion.

Refining margins were a major driver, reported at about $50 a barrel, alongside high crude prices with Brent near $117 while traffic through the Strait of Hormuz remains disrupted. The results mirror the pattern of earlier quarters this year, in which the war has lifted earnings across the large producers.

For drivers and households, the same conditions that produce these profits are the ones keeping gasoline above $4 in states including Ohio, which has become a campaign issue in the final days before the midterms. Energy costs were among the most cited concerns in final polling.

Watch whether an agreement to reopen Hormuz, which Iran floated on Sunday, changes the price outlook, and how the companies guide spending for 2027.

items.title: How news organizations will call Tuesday's races, with the first calls expected at 6 p.m.
items.summary:
News organizations are preparing to call hundreds of races on Tuesday night with more than 4,000 Associated Press staff and stringers reporting results from across the country. The first calls are expected when polls close in Indiana and Kentucky at 6 p.m. Eastern.

The AP and the networks base calls on vote counts, exit and survey data, and the remaining ballots to be counted, and they do not call a race until they are confident the trailing candidate cannot catch up. This year that work is complicated by the legal fights over mail ballots in states including California, and by the large number of races expected to be decided by very small margins.

Control of both chambers is in play, and forecasters count dozens of House races and seven Senate races as toss-ups or near them. A long night is likely, and some close races may not be called until Wednesday or later as mail and provisional ballots are counted.

Watch the early calls in Indiana and Kentucky for the first signal of turnout patterns, and Ohio's Senate race, which is among the last expected to be resolved.

items.title: Browns get run over in Pittsburgh, fall 27-6 to the Steelers
items.summary:
The Steelers beat the Browns 27-6 on Sunday at Acrisure Stadium, in a game both teams entered at 5-2 with first place in the AFC North on the line. Pittsburgh leaves at 6-2 and alone in first, Cleveland drops to 5-3, and the Browns never reached the end zone, scoring only on two Andre Szmyt field goals while trailing 20-6 at halftime.

Pittsburgh ran for about 200 yards. Jaylen Warren carried 17 times for 143 yards and a touchdown, Rico Dowdle added 56 yards and a score, and Pat Freiermuth caught a short touchdown just before halftime. Deshaun Watson threw for a season-high 324 yards but was sacked eight times and lost a fumble. Harold Fannin Jr. was the lone bright spot with 10 catches for 154 yards, while Quinshon Judkins was held to 25 rushing yards and Cleveland totaled only 34 yards on the ground. It was Pittsburgh's 23rd straight regular-season home win over Cleveland.

The loss splits the season series, so the Browns have no head-to-head game left to close the gap, and it exposed problems that have followed them all season: slow starts, a run defense that gave up 160 rushing yards in the first half alone, and an offensive line under pressure heading into the trade deadline.

Next up is a trip to New Orleans on Sunday, November 8, at 1 p.m., followed by Houston at home on November 15.

items.title: Mobley and Allen power the Cavs' 136-111 rout in Milwaukee — the Thunder come to Rocket Arena Monday
items.summary:
The Cavaliers beat the Bucks 136-111 on Saturday night in Milwaukee, their first blowout win and first road win of the season. Evan Mobley scored 27 points and Jarrett Allen added 25 points and 11 rebounds, combining for 52 points, as Cleveland improved to 4-2.

Milwaukee led after the first quarter, then Cleveland scored 48 points in the second quarter to lead 72-46 at halftime while shooting 62 percent. The lead reached 34 points in the second half, with 60 points scored in the paint. Donovan Mitchell added 15 points and James Harden 13 with 7 assists, so neither guard had to carry the offense.

Coach Kenny Atkinson said the plan came from morning film study: feed the big men early and often. It is the clearest picture yet of what Cleveland looks like when its frontcourt, rather than its star guards, drives the game, and Mobley is averaging a career-high 19.7 points.

Next is Oklahoma City at Rocket Arena on Monday at 7 p.m., followed by a return game in Oklahoma City on Wednesday. The Thunder are missing several key players, including Chet Holmgren and Jalen Williams.

items.title: Ohio State regroups after a 30-18 loss at USC, with a safety admitting a 'lack of effort' on the opening score
items.summary:
Ohio State lost 30-18 at USC on Saturday night, falling to 6-2 in what was Lincoln Riley's biggest Big Ten win at USC. It is the first time Ohio State has lost two games this early in a season since 2011, and it leaves the Buckeyes with almost no margin left in the playoff race.

The numbers were strange. Ohio State outgained USC 464 yards to 338, held the ball for more than 39 minutes, and still scored only one touchdown while kicking four field goals, stalling repeatedly near the goal line. USC scored on its second play, a 69-yard catch and run 39 seconds into the game. Starting safety Jaylen McClain said Sunday there was a little bit of lack of effort on that play, while calling the rest mostly bad execution. The Buckeyes were also flagged 11 times.

Ohio State played without starting quarterback Julian Sayin, who hurt his shoulder in October. True freshman Luke Fahey made his first start and threw for 260 yards and one touchdown with no turnovers. Jeremiah Smith caught 10 passes for 83 yards and scored the 40th touchdown of his career, a Big Ten record.

The Buckeyes must now be near-perfect the rest of the way. Next they host Oregon at home on Saturday.

items.title: Last call for early voting in Ohio: Sunday 1 to 5 p.m., no voting Monday, mail ballots due Tuesday at 7:30 p.m.
items.summary:
Sunday was the final day of in-person early voting in Ohio, from 1 to 5 p.m. only, at county boards of elections. In Cuyahoga County that is the Board of Elections at 1803 Superior Avenue in Cleveland. There is no early in-person voting on Monday, and Election Day is Tuesday, with polls open from 6:30 a.m. to 7:30 p.m.

About 235,500 Ohioans had requested mail ballots and not yet returned them in the most recent state reporting. Secretary of State Frank LaRose urged those voters not to mail them now, and to use the drop box outside their county board or hand the ballot to an elections worker instead. Ballots must now be received by 7:30 p.m. on Tuesday. Ohio no longer counts ballots that arrive after Election Day, under a law passed last year.

Turnout is already near record levels. About 1.19 million Ohioans had voted early in the latest reporting, on pace to pass the 2022 midterm record of 1.47 million early votes. Photo identification is required in person, and voters who requested a mail ballot but want to vote in person on Election Day can only do so by provisional ballot.

If you still hold a mail ballot, the drop box is the safe route before Tuesday evening.

items.title: Ohio decides Tuesday: the Brown-Husted Senate race is a toss-up and the governor's race is down to the wire
items.summary:
Ohio voters decide Tuesday whether to keep appointed Republican Senator Jon Husted or send former Democratic Senator Sherrod Brown back to Washington. It is a special election for the seat JD Vance left to become vice president, and the winner serves through January 2029. The Cook Political Report rates it a toss-up, one of seven nationally, with Senate control in the balance.

Polling tilts slightly toward Brown. Averages put him ahead by about 2.6 points, and a Suffolk University survey had him at 47 percent to Husted's 44. Campaigns and outside groups have spent roughly $500 million on advertising. Brown is running on costs and corporate power, Husted on business rankings and the 2025 tax law, and both have fought over data centers, which Brown blames for rising electric bills. Two minor candidates polling around 3 percent combined could matter in a race this close.

The governor's race has been even rougher. Democrat Amy Acton, Governor Mike DeWine's former health director, led Republican Vivek Ramaswamy by an average of about 4.3 points in late polling. An ad featuring Acton's estranged mother drew backlash and was off Ohio airwaves by October 29, and Acton answered at a Cleveland rally headlined by Barack Obama.

Watch turnout on Tuesday. With both races this close, the early-vote lead Democrats built could be tested by Election Day voting.

items.title: The Guardians' winter begins with a rotation hole, and a former ace is floated as an affordable fix
items.summary:
Cleveland enters the offseason needing dependable innings. Foster Griffin is a free agent and is expected to price himself beyond what the Guardians usually pay, leaving a hole behind Gavin Williams, Tanner Bibee and Parker Messick in the rotation.

One affordable name being floated is Walker Buehler, a free agent again after a bounce-back season in San Diego. He went 9-6 with a 4.63 earned run average over 32 starts and 153 and two-thirds innings, with 131 strikeouts, his heaviest workload since 2021 after two major elbow surgeries. He signed last winter on a small guaranteed deal after a rough 2025 that included a release from Boston.

Buehler is not the pitcher who went 16-4 for the Dodgers in 2021 and won two World Series rings. His strikeout rate is down and he allows more home runs than he once did. But Cleveland has a long record of reviving veteran pitchers on short, cheap deals, and a one-year contract for back-of-the-rotation innings fits that pattern.

The other half of fixing the rotation is internal: Bibee, who led the team with 188 innings despite a 7-15 record, said he expects to bounce back next year.

baby.tip: For the first hours after birth, skin-to-skin contact is the main event: baby on a parent's chest helps regulate the baby's temperature, breathing and blood sugar, and it is something Mike can do too, not just Kelly. Keep the hospital bag's long phone charger within reach, drink water whenever it's offered, and let the nurses set the pace — resting while the baby rests starts now, not at home.
baby.fact: A newborn's stomach is tiny — about the size of a cherry on day one, holding roughly a teaspoon or two at a time. That is why brand-new babies feed so often, and why frequent small feeds in the first days are exactly right rather than a sign something is wrong.
baby.fun: Today's tiny prep mission, hospital edition: start the notes-app list neither of you will remember later — first song played for the baby, the weather outside (cloudy and in the upper 60s in Solon), and one line about how each of you is feeling. Future you will be very glad past you bothered.
